questions.q: Why is std::chrono::steady_clock generally preferred over std::chrono::system_clock for measuring elapsed time?
options: steady_clock has nanosecond precision and system_clock does not
steady_clock is guaranteed monotonic and never jumps backward, while system_clock can be adjusted (e.g. by NTP synchronization)
system_clock cannot be used with duration_cast
steady_clock is the only clock available on Windows
questions.explain: system_clock represents wall-clock time and can be adjusted by the OS or NTP, potentially jumping forward or backward. steady_clock (and high_resolution_clock, typically backed by it) is monotonic, making it reliable for measuring elapsed durations.

questions.q: In a naive benchmark loop that computes a value but never uses it, what can an optimizing compiler legally do?
options: Nothing — the compiler must always execute every line written
Delete the entire computation, since its result has no observable effect on the program
Automatically replace it with a call to Google Benchmark
Convert the loop into a separate thread
questions.explain: If a computed value is never used in any way the compiler can observe, the compiler is permitted to eliminate the dead code entirely via dead-code elimination, making the benchmark measure essentially nothing.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a 'warm-up' pass before the timed region of a benchmark?
options: To let the CPU physically heat up for better performance
To avoid including the one-time costs of cold cache and an unlearned branch predictor in the timed measurement
To trigger garbage collection before timing begins
To verify the function compiles correctly
questions.explain: The first call(s) to a function pay extra cost because instructions/data aren't yet in cache and the branch predictor hasn't learned the function's typical behavior. A discarded warm-up run avoids attributing that one-time cost to the timed measurement.

questions.q: What does benchmark::DoNotOptimize(result) do in a Google Benchmark test?
options: It disables all compiler optimizations for the entire program
It prevents the compiler from eliminating the computation of `result` as dead code
It forces the benchmark to run on multiple threads
It converts `result` into an atomic variable
questions.explain: DoNotOptimize marks a value as used in a way the optimizer must respect, preventing the compiler from proving the computation has no effect and deleting it — directly solving the dead-code-elimination trap.

questions.q: Why is timing a single call that takes about 50 nanoseconds unreliable with a basic std::chrono measurement?
options: std::chrono cannot represent durations shorter than one second
The duration being measured can be comparable to or smaller than the clock's own measurement overhead and noise
Nanosecond durations always round to zero
high_resolution_clock only updates once per millisecond on all platforms
questions.explain: When the measured operation is extremely short, the overhead and granularity of the timing mechanism itself can be a significant fraction of (or larger than) the quantity being measured, making a single measurement unreliable. Running many iterations and averaging mitigates this.
